rewritten_text:
Those were the finest times, those were the darkest times; it was an age of good sense, an age of folly, an era of faith, an era of disbelief, a season of Light, a season of Darkness, a springtime of expectation, a winter of hopelessness. Everything lay ahead of us, nothing lay ahead of us; we were all travelling straight to Heaven, we were all travelling straight in the contrary direction. In brief, the period so resembled our own that certain of its loudest authorities demanded that, whether praised or condemned, it should be described only in the most extreme terms.

England’s throne held a king of ample jaw and a queen of unremarkable face; France’s throne held a king of ample jaw and a queen of lovely face. In either land, the masters of those State preserves where loaves and fishes abounded considered it more transparent than crystal that the general arrangement of things was fixed for eternity.

The year was one thousand seven hundred and seventy-five of Our Lord. England was granted spiritual revelations in that privileged time, just as she is now. Mrs. Southcott had lately celebrated her blessed twenty-fifth birthday; a prophetic private of the Life Guards had announced her exalted advent by proclaiming that preparations were complete for London and Westminster to be swallowed whole. A mere dozen years had elapsed since the Cock-lane ghost was put to rest, having knocked out its communications much as the spirits of this very past year, supernaturally wanting in invention, knocked out theirs. Communications of an entirely earthly nature had recently reached the English Crown and People from a congress of British subjects in America. These, curiously enough, have turned out to matter more to humanity than any intelligence so far delivered by the offspring of the Cock-lane brood.

France, generally less blessed in spiritual affairs than her sister bearing shield and trident, slid downhill with extraordinary ease, producing paper money and spending it. Directed by her Christian shepherds, she also amused herself with humane accomplishments such as condemning a young man to have his hands severed, his tongue plucked out with pincers, and his body burned alive. His offence was failing to kneel in the rain before a filthy procession of monks that passed within sight, some fifty or sixty yards away. It seems likely that, when this sufferer was killed, trees stood growing in the forests of France and Norway which Fate, the Woodman, had already selected for felling and sawing into planks. From those planks would be built a certain portable framework containing a sack and a blade, a structure destined to become dreadful in history.

‘Well, that’s how everybody lives, Huck.’

‘Tom, that doesn’t matter. I’m not everybody, and I can’t stand it. It’s awful having so many rules. And food comes too easily—I don’t care about eating when it’s like that. I have to ask before I go fishing, and ask before I go swimming. Darn it, I have to ask before I do anything. And I had to talk so politely I couldn’t enjoy myself. Every day I had to go up into the attic and swear for a while, just to get the taste back in my mouth, or I’d have died, Tom. The widow wouldn’t let me smoke. She wouldn’t let me shout, or yawn, or stretch, or scratch myself in front of people—’ Then, with a burst of particular anger and hurt, he added, ‘And darn her, she prayed all the time! I never saw a woman like her! I had to leave, Tom. I just had to. Besides, school’s going to start, and I’d have had to go. Well, I wasn’t putting up with that, Tom. Listen, being rich isn’t nearly as good as people say. It’s nothing but worry and hard work, and wishing you were dead all the time. These clothes suit me, and this barrel suits me, and I’m never giving them up again. Tom, none of this trouble would have happened without that money. Just take my share along with yours, and give me a ten-cent coin now and then—not too often, because I don’t care about anything unless it’s pretty hard to get. And go ask the widow to let me off.’

‘Oh, Huck, you know I can’t do that. It wouldn’t be fair. Besides, if you give it a little more time, you’ll start to like it.’

‘Like it! Sure—the way I’d like a hot stove if I sat on it long enough. No, Tom, I won’t be rich, and I won’t live in those cursed, stuffy houses. I like the woods, and the river, and big barrels, and I’m sticking with them. Darn it all! We’d just got guns and a cave, everything ready to be robbers, and then this stupid business had to come along and spoil it!’

Tom spotted his chance.

‘Listen, Huck, being rich won’t stop me becoming a robber.’

‘Really? Oh, wonderful! Are you absolutely serious, Tom?’

‘As serious as I am sitting here. But Huck, we can’t let you join the gang unless you’re respectable, you know.’

Huck’s delight vanished.

‘You can’t let me in, Tom?’

‘Are you listening to me? I have learned the language of despair; I know every word by heart, because I am Despair itself. And what a strange creature I am: joyful, triumphant Despair. But those words are untrue, for the wave may be dark, yet it is not bitter. We lie down and close our eyes with a gentle good night, and when we wake, we are free. Come, then, stop hesitating! See this pleasant drink! Look at me: it is a benevolent spirit inviting you, not a mortal girl, saying in persuasive tones—oh, if only they could persuade you!—Come and drink.’

As I spoke, I kept my eyes on his face. His exquisite beauty, the heavenly compassion shining in his eyes, and his gentle but earnest expression of protest and wonder changed my overwrought feelings before he said a word. They stripped away all the hardness of despair and left me filled with the tenderest grief. I saw that his eyes, too, were wet as he took both my hands in his. Sitting down beside me, he said:

‘You would lead me into a sorrowful act, my dearest friend. Your suffering must indeed be profound to fill your mind with such unhappy thoughts. You long for death, yet you fear it, and you want me beside you. But I am less courageous than you; even with your company, I dare not die. Hear me first, and then consider whether you ought to persuade me to join your plan, even if despair’s overwhelming eloquence could make dark death so attractive that the beautiful heavens seemed dark by comparison. Please listen to someone who has himself harboured desperate thoughts and yearned impatiently for death, but who has finally trampled that phantom underfoot and destroyed its sting. Come: since you have played Despair with me, I shall play Una with you and lead you unharmed out of his dark cavern. Listen, and allow yourself to be moved by words that contain no trace of selfish passion.

‘We do not know the meaning of this vast world, with its strange mixture of good and evil. But we have been placed here and told to live and hope. I do not know what we should hope for; still, there is some good beyond ourselves that we must seek, and that is our task on earth. If misfortune attacks us, we must fight it, thrust it aside, and continue searching for what we are made to desire. I cannot say whether this promise of future good prepares us for another existence, or whether it simply means that, as workers in God’s vineyard, we must help make the road easier for those who come after us.’
